input.question: Salts are constantly added to the ocean through volcanic emissions, runoff from continents, and the weathering of rocks in general, but is there any process that reverses this and removes it?
input.ground_truth: Yes. Salt can settle out, be captured by organic processes, and (most commonly) become landlocked. In that last one, a part of the ocean recedes or gets cut off from the rest of the ocean. The water evaporates and deposits the salt (which gets buried over time), then the fresh water rains back into the rest of the ocean.

response.prediction:
Sure! Let’s imagine the ocean is like a big bathtub full of water, and sometimes we sprinkle in little bits of salt (like when you add salt to your bath, but way smaller pieces!). These tiny salt pieces come from volcanoes, rain that runs off the land, and rocks getting worn down.

But, do we ever take the salt out of the bathtub? Yes, we do! Here’s how:

Sometimes, water from the ocean evaporates—this means the sun heats the water and turns it into vapor that goes up into the sky as clouds. But the salt is too heavy to go up with the water, so it stays behind in the ocean. Over a very, very long time, this means the salt can get left behind or get trapped in special layers underground. Also, some salt can get stuck in the shells of tiny sea creatures when they die and sink to the bottom of the ocean.

So, even though we keep adding salt, some of it also gets left behind or hidden away, kind of like how your toys can get lost under the bed! That’s how the ocean keeps just the right amount of salt.
